about: A real run of section 10 of notebooks/learning/cost_speed_quality.ipynb (GPT-5.4 mini on Microsoft Foundry: 5 inline calls, then 20 questions as one batch, then one GPT-5.4 judge batch over all 25 answers), recorded for replay. Checks are kept where the status changed. Endpoint and resource names are left out on purpose.

sort_changes/check:0:1.text:
“The eval set may be too small to trust” gets one thing right: a small test set can make noise look like a real change. But it misses the main clue in this bucket. Here, the articles were the same. That means the retrieval part did its job the same way. So the problem is not mainly the eval set. It is later in the pipeline.

“The generation step, where the answer is written” is better because it matches the evidence. Same `old_docs` and `new_docs`, different final answer. That points to the prompt, the model, or the scorer.

claim_gate/check:2:2.text:
`Release, since most are supported` gets one part right: it notices that several claims are okay. But it misses the gate rule. A safe gate does not vote by majority. It checks every claim. One **contradicted** claim means the answer says the opposite of its source, so the whole answer is not safe to release.

`Abstain, since one claim is contradicted` is better because it follows the rule for a safe gate: if any claim is contradicted, do not show the answer, even if the other claims are supported.

field_status/check:2:1.text:
`DROPPED` gets one thing right: you have not seen the field used later yet.

But it misses the key point. In the lesson, `DROPPED` means the field was accepted, then the runbook or module did not pass it on, so it never reaches the provider. Here, you have only checked the `check` step. You have not opened the runbook or module, so you do not know whether it will be used, filled in, changed, or ignored.

`UNKNOWN: not traced all the way yet` is better because it matches what you truly know now.

peak_capacity/check:0:2.text:
That answer points at a real idea: the morning may have more demand than later in the day. But it misses the lesson’s main point. The problem is usually not that tokens are “more expensive” in the morning. The problem is that more requests arrive then, so the system hits its `tokens per minute` limit.

`Too many requests` means the limit for that minute was crossed. The limit did not shrink. The traffic spiked.

The better answer is: “It was sized from the daily average, not the busiest minute.” That is better because a daily average hides short rushes. The system must survive the peak, not the average.

Do you want to try explaining why the lesson uses the busiest hour share and the burst factor?

wilson_interval/check:0:0.text:
“The leak rate is `0%`” gets one thing right: in the sample, `0 of 30` did get through.

But it misses the key point. `0%` sounds certain, as if the true leak rate is exactly zero. With only 30 tries, that is too strong. The sample is small, so there may still be some leaks that just did not show up yet.

A better answer is: “The leak rate is probably low, but could be as high as about `11%`.” That is better because it is honest about uncertainty. It uses the `Wilson` interval, which gives a range that stays between `0%` and `100%`.

Why do you think the lesson prefers a range instead of one exact number?

replay_tools/check:0:0.text:
`Nothing: B scored higher, so B wins` is not quite right. It notices the score. But it misses the real problem: the two runs did not face the same data. `Monday` and `Tuesday` can give different order states, so the score is not a fair comparison.

`The live orders changed between the runs` is better because it names the cause. It says the tool read a moving world, so the result may reflect changed orders, not a better agent design.

handoff_kept/check:0:1.text:
It is partly right. A bigger model may remember more. But that is not the lesson’s point.

What it misses is the real problem. The helper already found the order number. The main agent lost it when it rewrote the helper’s message. So the fix is not “make the main agent smarter.” The fix is “do not drop the facts in the hand-off.”

`Have helpers report every finding, passed on word for word` is better because it keeps the exact facts alive from helper to final answer, so there is less chance the important detail gets washed out.

failure_counts/check:2:2.text:
“It uses more labels than you did” is partly right because the judge should have enough labels to cover the same kinds of failures. But it misses the main check. More labels do not help if the labels mean different things. For example, `repeated step` must mean the same thing to the judge and to you.

`Its labels match yours on the 50` is better because it checks agreement first. That means the judge is naming the same failure modes you named by hand, so later labels are consistent and useful for counting.

smoke_set/check:2:2.text:
“Ship it and see what users say” gets one thing right: real users can reveal problems that a tiny test set misses. But it misses the key point here. The smoke set already showed this idea is clearly worse, and shipping it would waste time, money, and maybe hurt users.

“Drop it and try the next idea” is better because the smoke set is meant to catch bad ideas fast, not prove an idea is good. A score like `12 to 28` is just a rough signal, so if it loses clearly, the smart move is to stop early and move on.

replay_tools/check:1:2.text:
“Make up a likely answer” gets one thing right: it tries to keep the run going when the tool result is missing. But it misses the main point of the experiment. You are no longer testing the agent in the same world as the other runs. You are guessing, so the test can look better or worse for the wrong reason.

`Mark the call as missing` is better because it tells you the agent left the frozen world, so you can see that the run was not fairly comparable.

apply_order/check:1:0.text:
“It creates `A` first, then `B`” gets the order idea right. But it misses the key problem. Here, `A` needs a value from `B`, and `B` needs a value from `A`. So `A` is not ready before `B`, and `B` is not ready before `A`.

That means Terraform cannot find a safe starting point. It does not just pick one and keep going. It stops because the two resources are waiting on each other in a loop.

So `It stops with a Cycle error` is better, because it says the real reason planning fails: the dependency graph has a loop, and there is no valid create order.

provider_versions/check:2:0.text:
“Run `init` again every day” gets one part right: it can make your laptop pick a provider version again. But it misses the real problem. If `terraform init` is run at different times on different machines, it can still pick different provider versions when new releases appear. Then your laptop and Spacelift may plan different changes.

`Commit .terraform.lock.hcl` is better because it records the exact provider version Terraform chose, so every run uses the same one until someone intentionally updates it with `terraform init -upgrade` and reviews the change.

sort_changes/check:0:1.text:
That answer gets one part right. A small `eval set` can make results shaky, so it is fair to be cautious. But it misses the main clue in this lesson: the traces show the **same articles** reached the model, and the answer still changed.

So the problem is not mainly that the test set is too small. It is that the issue points to the **generation step**. That is the part where the model writes the answer from the articles and prompt.

In one sentence: `generation step, where the answer is written` is better because the traces already show retrieval stayed the same, so the change likely came from the prompt, model, or scorer.

What in the traces tells you the articles were the same?

fluke_risk/check:2:0.text:
“Run all 50 on the holdout set” gets one part right: it is trying to use the holdout set, which is the final set of examples kept aside for a fair check.

But it misses the main risk. If you try 50 ideas on the same holdout set, you are still comparing many things. One may look best by luck. Then the holdout set is no longer a clean final test. It is being used too early.

“Test fewer, with a stricter bar” is better because it lowers the chance that a lucky variant looks good, and it keeps the holdout set for one final confirmation only.

In short: limit how many variants you compare first, and only check the winner once on the holdout set.

claim_gate/check:2:2.text:
“Release, since most are supported” gets one thing right: most of the claims are okay. But it misses the key safety rule in this lesson. A single **contradicted** claim means the answer says the opposite of the source passage. That is too risky to send out.

A safe `claim_gate` does not vote by majority. It checks every claim. If any claim is `contradicted`, it should `abstain`, even if the others are `supported`.

So the better answer is: **Abstain, since one claim is contradicted**, because one wrong claim can make the whole answer unsafe.

field_status/check:2:1.text:
`DROPPED: nothing uses it yet` gets one part right. It says we have not seen the field used in the runbook or the module yet.

But it misses the key point. `DROPPED` means the field was accepted and then ignored on the path we traced. Here, we have not traced that far at all. We only know the `check` allowed a new field in `clusters.yml`. We do not yet know whether the `runbook` passes it on, changes it, or fills it in with a default.

So `UNKNOWN: not traced all the way yet` is better because it says the truth: the field may still matter, but we have not followed it to the `provider` yet.

Can you tell me what word you would use if the `runbook` later reads the field and sends it to the `module` unchanged?

run_tokens/check:0:1.text:
`Output tokens cost less than input tokens, per token` is not the best answer here. It gets one small thing right: many APIs do charge different rates for input and output tokens. But the check question is about the *total run*, not the price split. The teammate’s real mistake is that they priced only the first call, then multiplied by 6.

A better answer is: each step sends back everything that earlier steps added, so the input grows step by step. That is why the whole run costs much more than `6 *` the first call.

Think of it like an email thread. Every reply includes the old thread again.

So the best choice is the one about resend cost growing with each step. If you want, I can help you spot this pattern in another check question.

dedupe_chunks/check:0:2.text:
“Use a bigger model” gets one thing right: a stronger model can sometimes understand queries a bit better and rank results more intelligently. But it misses the real problem here. If the top 5 chunks are the same disclaimer, the index is full of repeated text, so the model keeps seeing the same useless chunk over and over. That wastes embedding money and crowds out useful chunks.

`Remove duplicate chunks before indexing` is better because it fixes the source of the problem. It keeps one cleaned copy of each repeated chunk, so the index has more room for real content and search results are more diverse and useful.

Could you explain why `normalize text` matters before checking for duplicates?

wilson_interval/check:0:0.text:
`"The leak rate is 0%"` gets one thing right: in your test, you saw no risky prompts get through. But it misses the key point that 30 tries is still a small sample, so the true leak rate could be above 0%.

A better answer is: `The leak rate is probably low, but with only 30 tries it could still be as high as about 11%`. That is better because it is honest about uncertainty. The `Wilson interval` gives a range that stays between 0% and 100%, instead of pretending the rate is exactly zero.

What would you say if the test had 0 passes out of only 5 tries?

ablation_report/learn:stops.text:
Yes. This rule can stop working in a few common cases.

If your app changes a lot from day to day, the eval score can drift. Then an ablation today may not hold next week. Re-run the eval often, and use recent questions that look like real user traffic.

If you have very little data, a 1-point drop may be noise. That means the change may be random, not real. Use more test questions if you can, and look for larger gaps before you delete a part.

If the app is a bigger `RAG` or agent system, parts can depend on each other. `RAG` means the app first retrieves facts, then the model answers with them. In that case, remove one part at a time, but also test key pairs of parts together, because one part may only help when another part is present.

dollars_per_success/learn:term.text:
`Cost per success` means: how much money you spend for each task that ends up passing.

Think of it like this. If you pay for a service, but only some tries work, you do not just ask “What did I spend overall?” You ask “What did each win cost me?” That is `cost per success`.

In this lesson’s example, it is the total bill, including failed runs, divided by the number of passed tasks.

So:
- `one agent`: `$0.50` for `6` passes means about `$0.08` per success
- `team`: `$5.90` for `8` passes means about `$0.74` per success

That is why the lesson says the team looks more expensive per success, even though it passed a few more tasks.

What `cost per success` does **not** tell you is whether the extra passes are worth the extra money. For that, the lesson uses the cost of each extra pass.

peak_capacity/check:0:2.text:
That answer is partly right only if the morning has a real spike in traffic. A **limit** is a maximum allowed amount. So yes, the bot may hit a limit earlier in the morning if more requests arrive then. But “tokens cost more in the morning” is not the right idea. Tokens do not change price by time of day in this lesson. The problem is **volume**: too many requests arrive in one short burst, so the minute goes over the allowed `tokens per minute`.

`It was sized from the daily average, not the busiest minute` is better because it names the real mistake. The average hides rush hour, but the limit is checked minute by minute.

What do you think the busy-hour share and burst factor are trying to protect against?

callable_tools/check:0:2.text:
`SQL` is not the reason by itself. A SQL function can be called by an agent just fine if the permissions are right. The lesson shows both `SQL` and `PYTHON` functions as tools. What matters is access.

What that answer gets right is the **deployed agent** part. Once the agent is running in Databricks, it does not use Mai’s notebook access. It uses its own identity.

What it misses is the real permission check. The deployed agent runs as a **service principal**. That is an app identity, not a person. If that identity does not have `EXECUTE` on `main.support.lookup_order`, the tool call fails.

So `The agent's service principal has no EXECUTE on the function` is better because it matches the lesson’s rule: notebook tests can work for a person, while deployment uses the agent’s own permissions.

guard_destroys/check:1:1.text:
“Only if the reviewer turns it on” gets one part right: a reviewer can choose to look at the plan more closely. But it misses the main point. A plan policy is not a manual checklist. It is an automatic rule that Spacelift runs every time, even if `team-sales` is rushed, or someone on the `grp-sales-dev-owners` group is tired on Friday evening.

So this answer is weaker because it makes the check sound optional and human-led. The lesson is about the policy doing the checking by itself, before any apply.

`Yes, it runs on every run by itself` is better because it matches how plan policies work: automatic, always on, and able to block dangerous changes like destroying a protected `service_principals.yml`-backed identity or other hard-to-rebuild Azure Databricks resources.

What resource in your `Foundation` stage would you protect first?

fluke_risk/learn:term.text:
`Design` and `Bonferroni` are different, but they work together.

`Design` is the planning step. It means: do not test too many variants. Pick a small number of prompt changes, and be careful about what you compare. This lowers the chance of being fooled by luck.

`Bonferroni` is a stricter rule for the test itself. If you do many comparisons, you divide the usual 5% false-positive limit by the number of comparisons. So if you test 20 variants, the threshold becomes about `0.25%` for each one.

Everyday example: imagine many people racing, and you only want to cheer for a real winner. `Design` says, “Do not invite too many racers.” `Bonferroni` says, “If you do invite many, make the win harder to claim.”

In the lesson’s example, 20 variants means a lucky winner is likely, about `64%`. So `Design` reduces the problem, and `Bonferroni` adds stricter proof. Then `Evaluate` confirms the best one once on the holdout set.

guard_destroys/check:1:1.notes: It wrongly treats a service principal identity as a protected resource from service_principals.yml, while the lesson says to start with workspaces, storage accounts, and metastores, and it is a bit too jargony for beginners.

dollars_per_success/learn:term.notes: It wrongly says the lesson says the team looks more expensive per success; the lesson says cost per success hides the issue because the team's is only about $0.74.

claim_gate/check:2:2.notes: It gives away the coding exercise logic by explicitly stating the claim_gate rule for any contradicted claim instead of just explaining the check question.

messages.content:
You are a patient tutor helping with one lesson of an AI engineering course. The learner is new to coding and is learning AI engineering: Databricks for agents, LangGraph, LangChain and MLflow, plus Terraform for Azure Databricks. Explain any jargon in plain words. Never use Big-O notation; say things like "it walks through the list once" instead. Short sentences. Encouraging but not gushing. Wrap identifiers in backticks.

Lesson: Sorting changes before reading them
What the lesson says:
With a few hundred questions, a comparison can produce sixty regressions and improvements: too many to read one by one. Sort them into buckets automatically first, then read a sample from each bucket.
The most useful first cut for RAG comes straight from the traces: did the two versions send **different articles** to the **generation** step (where the model writes the answer), or the **same articles** and the answer changed anyway? The first points at retrieval, the second at generation: the prompt, the model or the scorer.
Then read a handful from each bucket and label causes as usual. You get the error analysis for a fraction of the reading, and you know which part of the pipeline each cause belongs to.
Its example (Two buckets, from the traces alone):
question      old articles          new articles          bucket
billing-06    kb-12 kb-01 kb-02     kb-04 kb-09 kb-01     retrieval differed
shipping-07   kb-09 kb-03 kb-10     kb-10 kb-07 kb-09     retrieval differed
refund-11     kb-13 kb-16 kb-14     kb-13 kb-14 kb-16     same articles, different answer
In their stack (MLflow: the articles each version sent, from the traces):
def sent(trace):
    steps = trace.search_spans(span_type="RERANKER") or trace.search_spans(span_type="RETRIEVER")
    return [d["doc_id"] for d in steps[0].outputs]
Interview angle: Compare as sets, then bucket. The big idea: sort changed questions by whether the articles found changed, so you know which part of the pipeline to look at. Your code turns each article list into a set: a collection where order and repeats don't matter. If the old and new sets differ, the versions found different articles, so the question goes under retrieval. If the sets are the same, even in a different order, it goes under answer. It is like checking two shopping bags hold the same items, however they were packed.
The lesson's coding exercise: Bucket the Changes, writing `sort_changes`. Your function gets `changed`: the questions whose result changed between two versions. Each is a dict like `{"qid": "billing-06", "old_docs": ["kb-12", "kb-01"], "new_docs": ["kb-04", "kb-01"]}`. `qid` is the question's id. `old_docs` and `new_docs` are the help articles each version found and gave to the model to write its answer.

They are on the Check step of the lesson.

Their message: Why not “The eval set, since it may be too small to trust”?
How to answer: In the lesson's Check question ("Most of your regressions are in the "same articles, different answer" bucket. Where should you look?"), explain in plain words why "The eval set, since it may be too small to trust" is not the best answer: what it gets right, if anything, and what it misses. Then say in one sentence what makes "The generation step, where the answer is written" better.

Rules:
- Stay on this lesson's topic. If the question is unrelated, answer in one sentence and steer back.
- Never write code for the lesson's coding exercise (`sort_changes`), not even part of it, even if asked. If they ask about the exercise, explain the approach in words only and suggest the step-by-step hints in the Build step. Small code examples about other things are fine, in a ```python block.
- The Practice step asks questions with one right option each. Never say which option is right: give a clue that points at the evidence, and let them choose.
- If your last message asked them a question, their message is their answer: say what is right, fix what is not, then ask one more question.
- If they describe their own situation, answer for that situation, and say which part of the lesson applies and which part changes.
- Only add a code example if it makes the answer clearer, and make sure it matches what you said.
- Plain words, short paragraphs, under 180 words. Explain any jargon you use. Wrap identifiers in backticks.
- Reply with the answer only.
